content: In infants born to mothers infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV), the average rate of HCV transmission is approximately 4%, regardless of whether the infant is breastfed or bottle-fed. Diagnostic criteria for perinatal HCV infection have not yet been established. Various patterns of anti-HCV antibodies have been observed in both infected and uninfected infants born to anti-HCV-positive mothers. Passively acquired maternal antibodies may persist in the infant for several months but are unlikely to remain beyond 12 months. HCV RNA can be detected as early as 1 to 2 months after birth. Recent studies indicate that injection drug use accounts for approximately 60% of HCV transmission in the United States. Thus, a potential risk factor can be identified in approximately 90% of individuals with HCV infection. In the remaining 10%, no recognized source of infection can be identified, although most individuals in this category are associated with low socioeconomic status. The only serologic tests currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for diagnosing HCV infection are those that detect anti-HCV antibodies. These tests identify anti-HCV in at least 97% of infected patients but cannot distinguish between acute, chronic, or resolved infections. The positive predictive value of enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for anti-HCV depends on the prevalence of HCV infection in the population and is lower in populations with an HCV prevalence of less than 10%. Supplemental testing with more specific assays, such as recombinant immunoblot assays, can confirm positive EIA results and prevent false-positive reporting, particularly in asymptomatic individuals. Supplemental test results may be reported as positive, negative, or indeterminate. An anti-HCV-positive individual is defined as one with both EIA-positive and supplemental test-positive results. Individuals with a negative EIA result or a positive EIA and negative supplemental test result are considered uninfected unless other evidence, such as abnormal ALT levels or unexplained liver disease, suggests HCV infection. Indeterminate supplemental test results may occur in recently infected individuals undergoing seroconversion or in those with chronic HCV infection. Indeterminate anti-HCV results may also indicate false positives, particularly in low-risk individuals. HCV infection can also be diagnosed by detecting HCV RNA using gene amplification techniques, such as reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). In rare cases, HCV RNA detection may be the only evidence of HCV infection. Although RT-PCR assay kits for HCV RNA are available for research purposes, none are FDA-approved. Many laboratories perform RT-PCR using in-house methods and reagents, and these assays are commonly used in clinical practice despite the lack of FDA approval. Most RT-PCR assays have a lower detection limit of 100 to 1,000 viral genome copies per milliliter. With proper optimization, 75% to 85% of anti-HCV-positive individuals and over 95% of those with acute or chronic hepatitis C will test positive for HCV RNA. Some HCV-infected individuals, particularly those with acute hepatitis C or end-stage liver disease, may intermittently test positive for HCV RNA. To minimize false-negative results, serum should be separated from cellular components within 2 to 4 hours of collection and stored frozen at -20°C or -70°C. Frozen samples should be protected from thawing during shipping. Quantitative assays for measuring HCV RNA levels, such as quantitative RT-PCR and branched DNA signal amplification assays, are available from commercial laboratories. These assays are not FDA-approved and are less sensitive than qualitative RT-PCR assays, with detection limits ranging from 500 viral genome copies per milliliter for the Amplicor HCV Monitor™ to 200,000 genome equivalents per milliliter for the Quantiplex™ HCV RNA Assay. Differences in assay standards preclude direct comparisons between these methods. Quantitative assays should not be used as primary tests to confirm or exclude HCV infection or to monitor treatment endpoints. Most individuals with chronic hepatitis C have circulating virus levels of 10^5 to 10^7 genome copies per milliliter. At least six different HCV genotypes and over 90 subtypes have been identified. Approximately 70% of HCV-infected individuals in the United States are infected with genotype 1, with subtype 1a being more common than subtype 1b. Commercial nucleic acid detection methods are available to classify HCV isolates by genotype and subtype. Limited evidence exists regarding differences in clinical features, disease outcomes, or progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) among individuals with different genotypes. However, responses to antiviral therapy vary by HCV genotype, with substantially lower response rates in patients infected with genotype 1 compared to other genotypes. Treatment regimens may differ based on genotype, and genotyping may be warranted for individuals with chronic hepatitis C being considered for antiviral therapy. Acute HCV infection is often asymptomatic or associated with mild clinical illness. Approximately 60% to 70% of individuals have no discernible symptoms, 20% to 30% may develop jaundice, and 10% to 20% may experience nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, or abdominal pain. Clinical illness in patients with acute hepatitis C who seek medical care resembles that of other types of viral hepatitis, necessitating serologic testing to determine the etiology of hepatitis in individual patients.
